note: Passing these finite behavioral checks is objective test evidence, not a complete code review or certification. Coding results are recorded separately from scenario mastery.

exercises.title: Parse exact money without floats
exercises.prompt: Implement parse_cents(text). Accept only ASCII digits with an optional dot followed by one or two digits. Return nonnegative integer cents. Reject signs, spaces, empty text, excess precision and non-strings with ValueError. Use integer arithmetic; 0 and leading zeros are valid. The tests inspect returned values and error types.

exercises.title: Build fresh category totals
exercises.prompt: Implement category_totals(rows). Each row is a dict with category (a nonblank string) and cents (a nonnegative int, excluding bool). Strip category whitespace and combine repeated names, preserving case. Return a fresh dict of integer totals. Empty input returns {}. Raise ValueError for invalid rows. Do not change the input rows. These finite checks test values and invalid cases, not every possible input.

exercises.title: Bound a retry delay
exercises.prompt: Implement retry_delay(attempt, cap). Both values must be positive ints, excluding bool; invalid values raise ValueError. Return min(2 ** (attempt - 1), cap) as integer seconds. Avoid constructing a huge power for a very large attempt. This function computes a delay only; it does not sleep or contact a service.

exercises.title: Keep customers with no paid orders
exercises.prompt: Write one PostgreSQL SELECT query. Return every customer, including customers with no paid orders. Sum total_cents only for orders whose status is paid. Use 0 when none qualify. Return columns customer_id and total_cents, ordered by customer_id ascending. Keep filtering from accidentally dropping unmatched customers.
exercises.starter:
-- Return customer_id and total_cents for every customer.
SELECT id AS customer_id, 0 AS total_cents
FROM customers
ORDER BY id;
exercises.schema:
customers(id integer PK, name text)
orders(id integer PK, customer_id integer FK, status text, total_cents integer)

tests.name: Paid, cancelled and no orders
tests.setup_sql: CREATE TABLE customers(id integer PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE orders(id integer PRIMARY KEY, customer_id integer REFERENCES customers(id), status text NOT NULL, total_cents integer NOT NULL);INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'A'),(2,'B'),(3,'C'); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,1,'paid',120),(2,1,'cancelled',999),(3,1,'paid',30),(4,2,'pending',50);

tests.name: Empty customer table
tests.setup_sql: CREATE TABLE customers(id integer PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE orders(id integer PRIMARY KEY, customer_id integer REFERENCES customers(id), status text NOT NULL, total_cents integer NOT NULL);

tests.name: Two matching paid orders
tests.setup_sql: CREATE TABLE customers(id integer PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE orders(id integer PRIMARY KEY, customer_id integer REFERENCES customers(id), status text NOT NULL, total_cents integer NOT NULL);INSERT INTO customers VALUES (4,'D'),(9,'E'); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,4,'paid',50),(2,4,'paid',50),(3,9,'cancelled',800);

exercises.title: Choose one latest event per order
exercises.prompt: Write one PostgreSQL SELECT query. Return one row per order_id with columns order_id and event_type, ordered by order_id ascending. The latest occurred_at wins; if two timestamps tie, the larger event id wins. A timestamp alone is not a unique tie-breaker.
exercises.schema: events(id integer PK, order_id integer, occurred_at timestamptz, event_type text)

tests.name: Timestamp tie
tests.setup_sql: CREATE TABLE events(id integer PRIMARY KEY, order_id integer NOT NULL, occurred_at timestamptz NOT NULL, event_type text NOT NULL);INSERT INTO events VALUES (1,10,'2026-01-01T00:00:00Z','created'),(2,10,'2026-01-02T00:00:00Z','paid'),(3,10,'2026-01-02T00:00:00Z','shipped'),(4,20,'2026-01-01T00:00:00Z','created');

tests.name: ID does not replace time ordering
tests.setup_sql: CREATE TABLE events(id integer PRIMARY KEY, order_id integer NOT NULL, occurred_at timestamptz NOT NULL, event_type text NOT NULL);INSERT INTO events VALUES (9,1,'2026-01-01T00:00:00Z','old'),(2,1,'2026-01-02T00:00:00Z','new');

tests.name: Empty events
tests.setup_sql: CREATE TABLE events(id integer PRIMARY KEY, order_id integer NOT NULL, occurred_at timestamptz NOT NULL, event_type text NOT NULL);

exercises.title: Filter outstanding invoices by tenant
exercises.prompt: Write one PostgreSQL SELECT query for tenant 7 only. Return unpaid invoices as columns invoice_id and amount_cents, ordered by invoice_id ascending. Rows from another tenant must never appear, even if their amounts look similar. This exercise checks query output; application authorization needs separate design and tests.
exercises.schema: invoices(id integer PK, tenant_id integer, amount_cents integer, paid boolean)

tests.name: Mixed tenants and payment states
tests.setup_sql: CREATE TABLE invoices(id integer PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id integer NOT NULL, amount_cents integer NOT NULL, paid boolean NOT NULL);INSERT INTO invoices VALUES (1,7,100,false),(2,8,100,false),(3,7,300,true),(4,7,50,false);

tests.name: Only another tenant has outstanding work
tests.setup_sql: CREATE TABLE invoices(id integer PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id integer NOT NULL, amount_cents integer NOT NULL, paid boolean NOT NULL);INSERT INTO invoices VALUES (1,8,90,false),(2,7,40,true);

tests.name: Zero amount is still an unpaid invoice
tests.setup_sql: CREATE TABLE invoices(id integer PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id integer NOT NULL, amount_cents integer NOT NULL, paid boolean NOT NULL);INSERT INTO invoices VALUES (7,7,0,false),(6,7,20,false);
